front_blocks.md: Define **externality**.

back_blocks.md: An **externality** occurs when there is an external impact on a **third party** not involved in the economic transaction.

front_blocks.md: Define **private cost**.

back_blocks.md: A **private cost** is what a producer **actually pays** to produce a good or service.

front_blocks.md: Define **external cost**.

back_blocks.md: An **external cost**, or **negative externality**, is the damage not factored into the economic activity, such as air pollution from producing electricity.

front_blocks.md: Define **private benefit**.

back_blocks.md: A **private benefit** is what a consumer **personally gains** from consuming a good or service.

front_blocks.md: Define **external benefit**.

back_blocks.md: An **external benefit**, or **positive externality**, is the benefit not factored into the economic activity, such as society gaining strong legal institutions when someone studies law.

front_blocks.md: When do external costs occur?

back_blocks.md: External costs occur when the **social costs** of an economic transaction are **greater than the private costs**.

cards.back_md: External costs occur when the **social costs** of an economic transaction are **greater than the private costs**.

cards.front_md: When do external benefits occur?
cards.back_md: External benefits occur when the **social benefits** of an economic transaction are **greater than the private benefits**.

front_blocks.md: Which two sides of the market can externalities affect?

back_blocks.md: Externalities can affect the **production side** (producer supply) and the **consumption side** (consumer demand) of the market.

cards.front_md: Which two sides of the market can externalities affect?
cards.back_md: Externalities can affect the **production side** (producer supply) and the **consumption side** (consumer demand) of the market.

Externalities can be either positive or negative.

back_blocks.md: **True.**
Externalities are spillover effects that can be either positive or negative for a third party.

front_blocks.md: Define **negative externality of production**.

back_blocks.md: A **negative externality of production** occurs whenever the production of a good or service generates **external costs**.

front_blocks.md: Define **over-provision**.

back_blocks.md: **Over-provision** is when the market produces too much of a good because producers consider only their **private costs** and not the **external costs**.

front_blocks.md: How can the external costs of steel production increase government spending?

back_blocks.md: The government may need to allocate additional funds for **healthcare** to treat pollution-related illnesses, such as respiratory diseases.

front_blocks.md: What happens to quantity and price if external costs are taken into account?

back_blocks.md: If external costs were considered, the quantity provided would **decrease** and the remaining units would be sold at a **higher price**.

front_blocks.md: How does the steel industry create external costs?

back_blocks.md: The steel industry emits **greenhouse gases** during production, contributing to **climate change** and posing health risks to vulnerable groups.

front_blocks.md: Give two external costs of mining iron ore.

back_blocks.md: External costs of mining iron ore include **soil erosion**, loss of habitat, decreased air quality and **chemical leakage into the water table**.
